tips.title: Eat the Rainbow
tips.content: Include fruits and vegetables of different colors in every meal. Each color provides unique vitamins and antioxidants your body needs.

tips.title: Stay Hydrated
tips.content: Aim for 8 glasses (2 liters) of water daily. Increase intake during exercise or hot weather. Your urine should be light yellow.

tips.title: Limit Processed Foods
tips.content: Reduce intake of ultra-processed foods high in sugar, salt, and unhealthy fats. Cook meals from whole ingredients when possible.

tips.title: Healthy Fats Matter
tips.content: Include sources of healthy fats like avocados, nuts, olive oil, and fatty fish (salmon, sardines). They support brain and heart health.

tips.title: Fiber is Essential
tips.content: Eat 25-30g of fiber daily from whole grains, legumes, fruits, and vegetables. Fiber aids digestion and helps maintain healthy cholesterol.

tips.title: Mindful Eating
tips.content: Eat slowly, chew thoroughly, and pay attention to hunger cues. This helps prevent overeating and improves digestion.

tips.title: Limit Added Sugar
tips.content: The WHO recommends less than 25g (6 teaspoons) of added sugar daily. Check labels — sugar hides in sauces, bread, and drinks.

tips.title: Protein at Every Meal
tips.content: Include a source of protein (eggs, lean meat, beans, tofu, dairy) at each meal to support muscle repair and keep you feeling full.

tips.title: 150 Minutes Per Week
tips.content: Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity (brisk walking, cycling) or 75 minutes of vigorous activity per week.

tips.title: Strength Training
tips.content: Include strength/resistance training at least 2 days per week. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, and boosts metabolism.

tips.title: Move Every Hour
tips.content: If you sit for long periods, stand up and move for at least 5 minutes every hour. Set a timer as a reminder.

tips.title: Warm Up & Cool Down
tips.content: Always warm up for 5-10 minutes before exercise and cool down afterward. This prevents injuries and aids recovery.

tips.title: Find What You Enjoy
tips.content: The best exercise is one you'll actually do consistently. Try different activities — dancing, swimming, hiking, yoga — until you find your fit.

tips.title: Stretch Daily
tips.content: Spend 10-15 minutes daily on flexibility exercises. Focus on major muscle groups, holding each stretch for 15-30 seconds.

tips.title: 7-9 Hours of Sleep
tips.content: Adults need 7-9 hours of quality sleep per night. Consistent sleep deprivation increases risk of heart disease, diabetes, and obesity.

tips.title: Consistent Sleep Schedule
tips.content: Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day — even on weekends. This regulates your internal clock.

tips.title: Digital Sunset
tips.content: Stop using screens (phone, TV, computer) at least 1 hour before bedtime. Blue light suppresses melatonin production.

tips.title: Cool, Dark, Quiet Room
tips.content: Optimal sleep temperature is 60-67°F (15-19°C). Use blackout curtains and consider white noise or earplugs.

tips.title: No Caffeine After 2 PM
tips.content: Caffeine has a half-life of 5-6 hours. Afternoon coffee can significantly disrupt your sleep quality.

tips.title: Bedtime Routine
tips.content: Create a relaxing pre-sleep routine: reading, gentle stretching, meditation, or warm bath. Signal your body it's time to wind down.

tips.title: Practice Mindfulness
tips.content: Spend 10 minutes daily in meditation or mindfulness. Apps like Headspace or Calm can guide beginners. It reduces stress and anxiety.

tips.title: Stay Socially Connected
tips.content: Maintain meaningful relationships. Loneliness is as harmful as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. Reach out to someone today.

tips.title: Set Boundaries
tips.content: Learn to say no. Overcommitting leads to burnout. Protect your time and energy for what matters most.

tips.title: Gratitude Practice
tips.content: Write down 3 things you're grateful for each day. This simple practice rewires your brain for positivity and reduces stress hormones.

tips.title: Seek Help When Needed
tips.content: There's no shame in talking to a therapist or counselor. Mental health is just as important as physical health.

tips.title: Limit News Consumption
tips.content: Constant news exposure increases anxiety. Set specific times to check news and avoid it before bedtime.

tips.title: Spend Time in Nature
tips.content: Even 20 minutes in green spaces reduces cortisol (stress hormone) levels. Take a walk in a park or garden.

tips.title: Annual Health Checkups
tips.content: Visit your doctor annually for preventive screenings, even when feeling healthy. Early detection saves lives.

tips.title: Know Your Numbers
tips.content: Track your blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, and BMI. Understanding your baseline helps catch changes early.

tips.title: Stay Up-to-Date on Vaccines
tips.content: Follow recommended vaccination schedules. Vaccines prevent serious diseases including flu, COVID-19, shingles, and pneumonia.

tips.title: Sunscreen Daily
tips.content: Apply broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen daily, even on cloudy days. Reapply every 2 hours outdoors. Skin cancer is highly preventable.

tips.title: Dental Health
tips.content: Brush twice daily, floss daily, and visit the dentist every 6 months. Poor dental health is linked to heart disease.

tips.title: Hand Hygiene
tips.content: Wash hands for 20 seconds with soap and water regularly. It's the single most effective way to prevent infections.

dailyFacts: Your brain uses about 20% of your body's total energy, despite being only 2% of your body weight.
The human heart beats approximately 100,000 times per day, pumping about 2,000 gallons of blood.
Your body produces about 25 million new cells each second. Every 13 seconds, you produce more cells than there are people in the US.
Laughing 100 times burns roughly the same number of calories as 10 minutes on a rowing machine.
The human nose can detect over 1 trillion different scents.
Your stomach gets a new lining every 3-4 days to prevent it from digesting itself.
Walking for just 30 minutes a day can reduce the risk of heart disease by 35-40%.
Human bones are 4 times stronger than concrete, ounce for ounce.
Your body contains enough iron to make a 3-inch nail.
The cornea is the only part of the body with no blood supply — it gets oxygen directly from the air.
A sneeze can travel at speeds up to 100 miles per hour.
Red blood cells make approximately 250,000 round trips through your body before returning to bone marrow to be recycled.
The average person walks the equivalent of 5 times around the Earth in their lifetime.
Your liver performs over 500 different functions, including filtering blood and producing bile.
Humans share about 60% of their DNA with bananas.
Exercise boosts the production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which helps grow new brain cells.
Just 10 minutes of sun exposure can provide your daily vitamin D requirement.
Stress doesn't just affect your mood — it physically shrinks your brain's prefrontal cortex.
Drinking water before meals can help with weight loss by reducing calorie intake by 75 calories per meal.
The microbiome in your gut contains 39 trillion bacteria — more than the number of human cells in your body.

categories.label: Underweight
categories.description: BMI below 18.5 may indicate nutritional deficiency. Consult a healthcare provider.

categories.label: Normal Weight
categories.description: Healthy BMI range. Maintain with balanced diet and regular exercise.

categories.label: Overweight
categories.description: Increased health risk. Consider dietary changes and increased physical activity.

categories.label: Obese (Class I)
categories.description: Moderate health risk. Consult a healthcare provider for a management plan.

categories.label: Obese (Class II)
categories.description: High health risk. Medical intervention recommended.

categories.label: Obese (Class III)
categories.description: Very high health risk. Seek comprehensive medical care.

bmiData.disclaimer: BMI is a screening tool and does not directly measure body fat or health. Athletes, elderly, and pregnant women may have misleading BMI readings.
